displayQuote: Two things are infinite: the universe and human stupidity; and I'm not sure about the universe

meta.title: Who really said "Two things are infinite: the universe and human stupidity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein. The line traces to Gestalt therapist Frederick 'Fritz' Perls, who published a version in 1947 crediting an unnamed 'great astronomer' — then, 22 years later, credited Einstein himself and added the famous punchline.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Two things are infinite: the universe and human stupidity'?
meta.ogDescription: Fritz Perls published it in 1947 crediting an unnamed astronomer, then attributed it to Einstein in 1969 and added the punchline. The whole attribution rests on his memory.

answer.label: Not Einstein — assembled by Fritz Perls between 1947 and 1969
answer.authorDates: 1893–1970 · German-born psychiatrist, founder of Gestalt therapy
answer.sourceLine: Perls printed the first half in 1947 and credited it to an unnamed “great astronomer” — not Einstein. Twenty-two years later, in 1969, he wrote “As Albert Einstein once said to me…” and, in a second book the same year, added the punchline about not being sure about the universe. The entire Einstein attribution rests on Perls’ recollection of a conversation, decades after the fact.

source.excerpt: Two things are infinite, as far as we know — the universe and human stupidity.
trail: The earliest known printing is Perls’ Ego, Hunger and Aggression (1947), p. 111 — and there the line is credited not to Einstein but to an unnamed ‘great astronomer’ Quote Investigator ↗.

In Gestalt Therapy Verbatim (1969), p. 33, Perls writes ‘As Albert Einstein once said to me: “Two things are infinite: the universe and human stupidity”’ — the first time the name appears anywhere full trace ↗.

The modern form, with the closing joke, appears in Perls’ In and Out the Garbage Pail (1969), p. 52: ‘…and I am not yet completely sure about the universe.’ Snopes reaches the same conclusion — no Einstein source exists Snopes ↗.
source.excerptNote: The line as Perls first published it in 1947 — no Einstein, no punchline. Both were added by Perls himself twenty-two years later.

All three Perls books — Ego, Hunger and Aggression (1947), Gestalt Therapy Verbatim (1969) and In and Out the Garbage Pail (1969) — remain protected, so quote a short excerpt with citation rather than reproducing passages. Note the practical trap: presenting the line as Einstein’s implies it is public domain, since Einstein’s own words have largely fallen out of copyright. It isn’t. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) is the default signature for any remark that sounds both clever and world-weary. The joke needs a speaker with the standing to pronounce on the size of the universe, and Einstein is the obvious candidate — which is presumably why Perls reached for his name in 1969, having managed without it in 1947. There is no record of the two men ever discussing the subject.

copyAttribution: Two things are infinite, as far as we know — the universe and human stupidity. —Frederick S. Perls, Ego, Hunger and Aggression (1947). Commonly misattributed to Albert Einstein.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually clean case, because the same author published the line three times over twenty-two years and the attribution changed each time — all of it in print, all of it dated.

items.why: Perls’ first printing credits the thought to an unnamed astronomer. If Einstein had said it to him, this was the moment to say so trace ↗.

items.who: “As Albert Einstein once said to me”
items.why: The Einstein attribution surfaces for the first time in Gestalt Therapy Verbatim, framed as personal recollection. No corroboration exists from Einstein’s side, and no such meeting is documented.
‘And I am not yet completely sure about the universe’ appears only in Perls’ second 1969 book — the funniest part of the quotation is the part furthest from any Einstein source Snopes ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Einstein. First published by Fritz Perls in 1947 crediting an unnamed astronomer, re-credited to Einstein by Perls in 1969, and completed with its punchline the same year full trace ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The joke works because of who is supposedly telling it. Coming from the man who measured the universe, ‘I’m not sure about the universe’ is a devastating throwaway; coming from anyone else it is merely a good line.
That is the mechanism behind a great many invented quotations: the wit is real, but it needs borrowed authority to land, and the borrowing is what makes it spread.
detailsBody: Perls, Ego, Hunger and Aggression (1947), p. 111: ‘Two things are infinite, as far as we know — the universe and human stupidity’ — credited to an unnamed great astronomer.
Perls, Gestalt Therapy Verbatim (1969), p. 33: ‘As Albert Einstein once said to me…’
Perls, In and Out the Garbage Pail (1969), p. 52: ‘…and I am not yet completely sure about the universe.’
Open question: whether the line also appears in the earlier 1942 South African edition of Ego, Hunger and Aggression has not been verified.
context.pull: In 1947 it was an unnamed astronomer. Only in 1969 did it become Einstein.
